question_text:
Art historian Ines Valcourt argues that a sarcophagus whose stone comes from the Vell Island quarry and whose carved hair shows drill-channel work can be assigned to the Perrin workshop of ancient Corvane. Chemical analysis has shown that the Dunmere sarcophagus is made of Vell Island marble. The hair on its figures, however, is so worn that it is impossible for now to tell whether drill channels were ever used. Thus, on Valcourt's criteria,

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: the sarcophagus was probably made by another workshop, since Vell Island stone alone cannot identify the Perrin workshop.
answer_b: the sarcophagus has not yet been shown to be Perrin work.
answer_c: the sarcophagus is probably Perrin work, since Vell Island stone is the rarer of the two features Valcourt requires.
answer_d: the sarcophagus would be ruled out as Perrin work should its hair prove to lack drill channels, since both features are required.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because Valcourt's criteria pair two features, Vell Island stone and drill-channel hair, as together enough for assigning a sarcophagus to the Perrin workshop. The text establishes only that the Dunmere sarcophagus meets the first feature; whether it meets the second cannot yet be determined because the hair is too worn. Since only one of the two features has been shown, the criteria do not yet support assigning the sarcophagus to the Perrin workshop. Nothing in the text says the sarcophagus is not Perrin work, only that it has not yet been shown to be.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This treats the lack of proof as proof against the assignment. The text says the hair is too worn to tell whether drill channels were used, so the sarcophagus may still turn out to meet both features; the stone alone is insufficient to settle the question, but it gives no reason to favor another workshop.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The text never says that Vell Island stone is rarer than drill-channel work, so this rests on an unsupported comparison. Even if it were true, meeting only one of the two features would not make the assignment probable on Valcourt's criteria.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. This reads the two features as both necessary for a Perrin assignment, but Valcourt says only that together they are enough to make the assignment. The text does not say that a sarcophagus lacking drill-channel hair could not be Perrin work by some other evidence, so it does not support ruling the sarcophagus out.

question_text:
Sports scientists tested whether a short jumping routine strengthens bones. They enrolled 56 girls, all aged 11 or 12, and randomly assigned half to do ten jumps each school day and half to do stretching for the same time. Bone growth is naturally rapid at these ages, and after eight months hip bone mineral content had risen in both groups, by 6.2 percent with jumping and 4.9 percent with stretching, a gap too large to attribute to chance. The researchers can most reasonably conclude that

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: the routine probably builds more bone than stretching does in girls of any age, since the jumping group's gain exceeded the stretching group's.
answer_b: the routine probably increased hip bone mineral content more than stretching did in girls of this age over the eight months of the study.
answer_c: the routine probably gives girls of this age a permanently higher bone mineral content than they would otherwise have had, since the jumping group finished ahead.
answer_d: the routine probably made no real difference in girls of this age, since bone mineral content was rising quickly in both groups during the eight months.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it claims only what the experiment supports. Girls aged 11 or 12 were randomly assigned to jumping or stretching, so the jumping group's larger rise in hip bone mineral content (6.2 percent versus 4.9 percent), a gap too large to attribute to chance, probably reflects the routine itself. The claim stays within the sample's age band, the hip measurement, and the eight-month period.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it overgeneralizes beyond the sample. Every participant was 11 or 12, and the text notes that bone growth is naturally rapid at these ages, so the result does not show that the routine builds more bone than stretching in girls of any age.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because bone mineral content was measured only at the end of eight months. The text gives no follow-up, so the result does not show that the advantage is permanent; it is true but not entailed that the jumping group finished ahead.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it reverses the conclusion. Bone mineral content did rise in both groups, as expected at these ages, but the jumping group's rise was larger by a gap too large to attribute to chance, and random assignment means normal growth cannot explain that difference.

question_text:
An observatory's scheduling committee divided 150 hours of telescope time among nine approved research projects for the coming semester, awarding every hour. Four of the projects study the Sun, and the committee's records show that those four together received no more than 38 hours. The committee has not yet published the individual awards for the other five projects, which were given the remaining hours. Therefore, on the basis of these figures,

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: each of the five projects that do not study the Sun received more than 20 hours.
answer_b: the five projects that do not study the Sun received an average of more than 25 hours each.
answer_c: at least one of the projects that do not study the Sun received more than 22 hours.
answer_d: the four projects that study the Sun together received less than a quarter of the 150 hours.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because the figures fix a minimum for the five projects that do not study the Sun. The four solar projects received at most 38 hours, so the other five received at least 150 - 38 = 112 hours together. If none of those five had received more than 22 hours, they could have received at most 5 x 22 = 110 hours together, which is less than 112. So at least one of them must have received more than 22 hours.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The figures set only a combined minimum of 112 hours for the five projects, not a minimum for each one. The committee could have given one project nearly all of those hours and the others very few, so it does not follow that every project received more than 20 hours.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The five projects received at least 112 hours together, which is an average of at least 22.4 hours, not more than 25. The average would exceed 25 only if the solar projects received fewer than 25 hours in all, and the text says only that they received no more than 38.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. A quarter of 150 hours is 37.5 hours, and the text says only that the solar projects received no more than 38 hours. They could have received exactly 38 hours, which is more than a quarter, so the figures do not guarantee that they received less than a quarter.

question_text:
In the Calder Valley, apple trees generally bloom later the higher they grow, since the air cools by roughly three degrees Fahrenheit for every thousand feet of elevation. At the Fennick orchard, however, trees planted at 900 feet bloom about a week later than trees planted at 1,400 feet on the same slope. Horticulturist Marisol Quint attributes the reversal to cold air that drains downhill on clear spring nights and settles around the lower trees. Quint's explanation would hold only if

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: the lower trees at Fennick belong to a variety that is naturally slower to bloom than the variety planted higher on the slope.
answer_b: the temperatures that a tree reaches overnight in early spring influence when it blooms, and not just the warmth it receives by day.
answer_c: orchards on other slopes in the Calder Valley also show trees at lower elevations blooming later than trees at higher elevations.
answer_d: the afternoon air at 900 feet at Fennick is warmer than the afternoon air at 1,400 feet during the early weeks of spring.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because Quint's explanation depends on cold air settling around the lower trees on spring nights. Her account can delay bloom at 900 feet only if overnight temperatures affect bloom timing. If bloom were set solely by daytime warmth, a nighttime pool of cold air would not matter, and the lower trees, which are warmer by day under the general pattern, would bloom earlier, not later, than the trees above them. So the explanation holds only if nighttime temperatures help determine when a tree blooms.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. A difference in variety would be a separate explanation for the later bloom of the lower trees, one that makes no use of drained cold air. Quint's explanation does not require it, and it would not be undermined if the varieties were the same.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. Other slopes showing the same reversal might fit a valley-wide cold-air effect, but Quint is explaining the pattern at Fennick, and her explanation would hold whether or not any other orchard shows it. This is true-but-not-required, not a necessary condition.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It simply restates the general pattern that lower air is warmer, which is the very pattern the anomaly contradicts. Quint's explanation would not fail if the afternoon air at 900 feet were not warmer, since colder afternoons at the lower trees would only add to the delay she describes.

question_text:
Two teams tested whether the fungicide Verdal slows bumblebee colony growth. In a laboratory study, Priya Nandakumar's team kept 24 colonies in screened cages for ten days, feeding half of them Verdal-treated syrup; treated and untreated colonies gained the same weight on average. In a field study, Lars Ekberg's team weighed 60 colonies placed beside orchards for a full spring; colonies beside Verdal-sprayed orchards gained less weight than those beside unsprayed orchards. Based on these results, it is reasonable to conclude that ...

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: the laboratory team probably weighed its colonies incorrectly, since any real effect of Verdal would have appeared within ten days.
answer_b: the laboratory result does not rule out a slowdown that emerges over a longer period, but the field result alone does not show that Verdal caused it.
answer_c: the field study shows that Verdal slows colony growth over a season, so the laboratory study's finding must have been mistaken.
answer_d: neither study offers useful evidence about Verdal, since two studies that reach different results cannot both be informative.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it accounts for both studies without discarding either. The laboratory study covered only ten days, so its finding of equal weight gain does not exclude an effect that builds up over a full spring. The field study compared colonies beside sprayed and unsprayed orchards, a difference that could involve more than Verdal, so its result alone does not establish that the fungicide caused the lower weight gain.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it claims a flaw the text does not support. Nothing in the passage suggests the laboratory team weighed its colonies incorrectly, and the assumption that any real effect would appear within ten days is not stated or implied; the study simply covered a much shorter span than the field study.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it picks a winner and goes too far. The field result shows that colonies beside sprayed orchards gained less weight, but the text does not establish that Verdal was the cause, and the laboratory finding can be accurate for its ten-day window without being mistaken.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it claims both studies are uninformative. Different results from studies with different designs and time spans do not make either study useless; each reports a real observation under its own conditions, and the difference between them is what points toward a longer-term or field-specific effect.

question_text:
Economist Ilse Brandvold argues that steam-powered curing sheds made nineteenth-century fishing cooperatives more profitable. Her evidence comes from the account books that a government survey gathered in 1900 from every cooperative then still in operation. Among the 30 cooperatives surveyed, the 18 that had installed steam sheds averaged yearly profits 40 percent above those of the 12 that had not. Brandvold concludes that steam sheds raised profits. Thus, the survey's figures alone

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: demonstrate that steam sheds raised profits, since a 40 percent gap between installers and non-installers is too large to attribute to chance.
answer_b: reflect self-selection, since only cooperatives that were already prospering could have afforded to install steam sheds in the first place.
answer_c: cannot show whether steam sheds raised profits across all cooperatives, since the books of cooperatives that closed earlier are missing from the comparison.
answer_d: are distorted by survivorship bias, so the true profit gap between installers and non-installers must have been smaller than 40 percent.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because the survey gathered books only from cooperatives still operating in 1900, so any cooperative that closed before then is absent from the comparison. The figures show that, among the cooperatives that lasted, installers earned more than non-installers. They say nothing about how steam sheds affected the cooperatives that closed, and those may differ systematically from the ones that remained. Thus the figures alone cannot show whether steam sheds raised profits across all cooperatives.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the size of the gap as decisive while ignoring what the survey left out. A large difference among 30 cooperatives that were all still operating in 1900 does not show what sheds did for cooperatives that closed earlier, whose books were never gathered.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it is not supported by the text. The passage says that installers earned more than non-installers but gives no information about whether the cooperatives were prospering before they installed sheds or whether prosperity was needed to afford them; this reverses the possible direction of cause without evidence.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because the text does not establish the direction of any distortion. The missing books could just as easily conceal a gap larger than 40 percent, or none at all; the passage supports only that the comparison is incomplete, not that the true gap was smaller. The technical term does not make the claim follow from the text.
